## 1. Summary

The Book of Mormon uses "it came to pass" far more often than the King James Bible. That is often
offered as evidence of a Hebrew original, because the phrase translates the Hebrew narrative form
*wayhi*. This report counts the Hebrew, not the KJV's English. It compares the two texts genre for
genre, and it splits each use by what follows the formula:

- **setting-first**: a time or circumstance comes first ("and it came to pass, *when* they had
  eaten, that…"). This is how Hebrew *wayhi* works as a narrative marker.
- **straight to the event**: the next thing that happened comes right after ("and it came to pass
  *that* they did march"). Hebrew *wayhi* doesn't do this.
- **ordinary verb** (Hebrew only): *wayhi* with its own subject ("and there was light"). No "it came
  to pass" renders it, so it's excluded.

Labels: **registered** results come from tests whose method and decision rule were written down and
hashed before the measurement ([`preregistrations/`](../preregistrations/)). Everything else is
**exploratory**. Each analysis's headline, as recorded in Requiem:

{{headlines}}

In the narrative frame (the book's own narration, without quotations and embedded speeches), the
Book of Mormon uses the formula {{v:frame-rate}} times per 1,000 words ({{v:frame-rate-1830}} in the
1830 text): {{v:frame-setting}} setting-first and {{v:frame-event}} straight to the event. Against
Hebrew setting-first *wayhi* in 17 matched narrative units, that is {{v:ratio-matched}} per 1,000
words, and {{v:ratio-per-verb}} per 100 verbs. The setting-first uses alone run at
{{v:setting-ratio}} the Hebrew rate. The difference is made up of the straight-to-the-event uses,
{{v:event-share}} of the book's total, a use Hebrew doesn't have.

On the Egyptian side, the texts that match the book in genre and date (connected narratives
composed before about 500 BC) run {{v:matched-range}} openings per 1,000 estimated translation
words, by text. That range brackets the book. The Lehi-era Demotic texts are lower but fail on
genre. So the Egyptian rate test is **inconclusive**, not negative. The two pre-registered tests
stand as registered: PREREG 2, {{v:prereg2-verdict}}; PREREG 30, {{v:prereg30-verdict}}.

## 4. Methods

### 4.1 Buckets and rules

Every use is put in a bucket by a rule that looks at the words right after the formula.

- **Hebrew rule** ([`src/bomstylo/hebrew.py`](../src/bomstylo/hebrew.py), `classify`). It reads the
  lemma and morphology of the next word or two:
  - setting-first if a setting word follows ("after", "when", "as", "end", "time", "if", "until",
    "before"), or a time noun after a preposition or numeral ("on the day", "at the end of
    days"), or a circumstantial clause (subject, then a participle, then a main verb later in the
    verse);
  - straight to the event if a finite verb follows directly (it never does with *wayhi*; the bucket
    exists so the absence is measured, not assumed);
  - ordinary verb otherwise.

  Forms: *wayhi* is morphology `HC/Vqw3ms` of lemma 1961 (*hayah*); its future counterpart
  *wehayah* ("and it shall come to pass") is `HC/Vqq3ms`.
- **English rule** ([`src/bomstylo/english.py`](../src/bomstylo/english.py)). It finds "it came to
  pass" and "it shall / should / will come to pass", and reads the next 40 characters. Two versions
  are kept and both are reported:
  - **registered**: PREREG 2's rule, unchanged. A short list of time words after the formula.
  - **revised**: the registered list plus settings that the calibrations below showed it missing
    ("the same day", "in process of time", "one day"…), relative conditions ("whosoever…"), and a
    setting placed just before the formula in the same clause ("And when the feast was ended, it
    came to pass…"). Every addition is a grammatical setting found by checking the rule against the
    KJV, where the Hebrew (or Greek) bucket is known. None was tuned on the Book of Mormon.
- **Calibration.** The English rule can only be trusted as far as it agrees with a reading whose
  answer is known:

{{calibration}}

### 4.2 Genre steps

The often-quoted comparison sets the whole Book of Mormon against the whole KJV Old Testament. That
mixes in poetry, law and prophecy, where the construction barely occurs. Here both sides are cut
the same way, one step at a time, and every step is reported:

| step | Old Testament side | Book of Mormon side |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | whole Old Testament | whole text |
| 2 | 17 narrative books (Genesis–Esther) | minus the KJV block quotations |
| 3 | story books: minus Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy (mostly law and address) | minus the KJV block quotations |
| 4 | story books, speech removed | narrative frame: minus embedded speeches, letters, prophecies and records |
| 5 | 17 named narrative units, speech removed | narrative frame |

- **Hebrew speech** is removed per instance. The KJV marks no quotations, so each Hebrew instance is
  placed at the same relative position in the World English Bible verse and checked against the
  WEB's quotation marks. Narrative-frame word counts use each verse's share of words outside quotes.
- **The 17 units** are connected narrative blocks as conventionally delimited, chapter-aligned.
  Whole books are too coarse: Genesis has genealogies, Exodus turns into law at chapter 20, Kings is
  padded with regnal formulae. **Daniel is left out on purpose**: its court tales are close
  analogues, but Daniel 2–7 is Aramaic, which has no *wayhi*, so it would read as a false zero.

{{hebrew-units}}

### 4.3 What the Book of Mormon side leaves out, and why

The comparison is about the book's own narration, so text the book takes from the KJV must not be
counted as its own. The layers are data in [`annotations/embedded.tsv`](../annotations/embedded.tsv),
read by [`src/bomstylo/spans.py`](../src/bomstylo/spans.py), not logic inside an analysis.

- **KJV block quotations** leave from step 2. These are the long Isaiah and Malachi chapters, which
  follow the KJV nearly word for word:

{{quotation-spans}}

- **Embedded speech** leaves at step 4: sermons, letters, prophecies and embedded records, as the
  book itself frames them. This also removes the KJV parallels inside speech, such as the Sermon at
  the Temple (3 Nephi 12–14, Matthew 5–7), Isaiah 29 in 2 Nephi 27, Isaiah 52 and Micah in
  3 Nephi 20–21, the Decalogue in Mosiah 12–13 and 1 Corinthians 13 in Moroni 7.
- **Zeniff's record** (Mosiah 9–10, the first-person part of the record the book embeds; chapters
  11–22 switch to third person and stay in the frame) is counted as speech,
  as in the earlier published figures. The registered PREREG 2 run counts it as frame, as
  registered. The sensitivity of every frame figure to this choice is reported in `bom-buckets`.
- **Checked against the texts.** The `exclusions` analysis finds every passage that shares long
  word runs with the KJV, and says at which step it leaves. Passages that stay in the frame are
  flagged in bold:

{{parallels}}

  Each passage is placed by the KJV book with the most shared runs. 1 Nephi 22:20 quotes the
  prophet-like-Moses saying, which the KJV has in Deuteronomy 18 and, nearest in wording, Acts 3.

### 4.4 Units and statistics

- **Per 1,000 words.** Book of Mormon rates use its own English words. Hebrew rates use the KJV's
  English words for the same verses (narrative frame: the WEB share outside quotes), so both sides
  are on an English scale. Demotic rates use words of the TLA's German translation; Egyptian token
  counts are scaled by the translation-words-per-token ratio measured in each TLA subset. These are
  not the same unit across languages. `per-verb` repeats the comparisons per 100 verbs, counted in
  each language's own text, and checks that verbs (unlike words) survive translation.
- **Intervals** are exact and 95%: Poisson (Garwood) for rates, Clopper–Pearson for shares, and the
  conditional binomial interval for rate ratios
  ([`src/bomstylo/stats.py`](../src/bomstylo/stats.py)).
- **Comparability of Egyptian texts.** An Egyptian rate counts for or against the book only against
  a text that matches it in genre (connected narrative) and date (composed about 600–500 BC or
  earlier; older is fine, because formal Egyptian kept the older literary register and Saite scribes
  revived it). Every Egyptian row carries date, genre and matched flags. When no matched text
  decides the question, the result is called inconclusive.

### 5.2 Forms of *wayhi* in the Hebrew Bible

{{about-hebrew-forms}}

The forms are easy to pool by accident: unpointed ויהי is also *wihi* ("and let it be"), and
unpointed והיה is also plain "and" + perfect. Pooling the past with the future (*wayhi* +
*wehayah* = {{v:pooled}}) compares two different constructions with one English phrase.

### 5.10 Egyptian

{{about-egyptian}}

The old narrative particles (ꜥḥꜥ.n, wn.ꞽn) are the unambiguous clause-opening "then" of Middle and
Late Egyptian narrative. Counting them is a floor: a text that chains events another way reads as
zero (Wenamun uses the Late Egyptian continuative instead). Demotic marks "it came to pass" with
ḫpr. Both lead into events, not settings.

{{res-egyptian}}

### 5.13 Pre-registered: PREREG 30, Joseph Smith's own "then"

{{about-prereg-jst-then}}

{{res-prereg-jst-then}}

Reading, from the pre-registration's Amendment 3: R1 shows that the straight-to-the-event idiom was
Joseph Smith's by 1830, in new narrative with no source text behind it. Every Smith narrative was
written after the Book of Mormon was dictated, so whether he had the idiom before it is untested.
No pre-1828 Smith narrative survives. Under the revised rule, formulas Smith kept from the KJV are
{{v:jst-kept-share}} straight to the event.

## 7. Limitations

- **The rules are word-after rules, not full readings.** Their agreement with the Hebrew, the Greek
  and a hand reading is in section 4.1: {{v:calibration-range}} of checked cases, lowest on future
  settings. The residual error is a few percent each way.
- **Speech removal is asymmetric.** The Old Testament side removes every quotation marked in the
  WEB. The Book of Mormon side removes sermons, letters and records, but not short dialogue inside
  narration. The book's frame therefore keeps some speech, which makes its frame rate, and the
  ratio, slightly conservative.
- **Versification.** The Hebrew text is numbered as in Hebrew Bibles, the KJV and WEB as in English
  ones. Hebrew instances in verses numbered differently can't be placed in or out of speech; they
  are counted as frame (`genre-ladder`). Single-form verses that don't match a KJV verse are left out
  of `kjv-rendering`.
- **The 1830 text is uncorrected OCR.** Uses removed after 1830 are restored from an alignment.
  {{v:reverse-absent}} current-text uses weren't found in the 1830 OCR by the aligner. An earlier
  hand check of these candidates found them present but garbled or misaligned (with 4 not found), but
  the per-case labels weren't kept, so the claim that no use was *added* after 1830 rests on an
  unrecorded check. Uses lost between the manuscripts and the 1830 printing are outside this
  study; Royal Skousen's critical text would settle them.
- **Three short KJV parallels stay in the frame** (section 4.3), together a few hundred words with
  one future-tense formula. They are reported, not removed, because they are short quotations inside
  narration, and the frame's rule removes framed speeches, not quotations.
- **Egyptian rates depend on scale factors.** Egyptian token counts are put on an English-word scale
  with a ratio measured in other texts of the same stage. Demotic rates are per German word. Neither
  scale has an interval. The per-verb comparison avoids this, but the TLA's VERB tag and the Hebrew
  verb tag haven't been validated against each other.
- **The Demotic selections are by rule.** TLA sentences have no text names, so narrative sentences
  are chosen from their German translations. The sentences are mostly from documents, later copies
  and a petition. That is why they fail on genre.
- **The Greek labels are one reader's.** 70 ἐγένετο were read in context and labelled by hand; the
  labels and their notes are in [`annotations/egeneto_labels.tsv`](../annotations/egeneto_labels.tsv).
- **The Greek is the SBLGNT, not the KJV's Textus Receptus.** Where the two Greek texts differ, an
  ἐγένετο may be missing from one side; those differences were not counted.
- **The WEB text drifts.** The pinned WEB build isn't archived; the current zip differs in one used
  verse (John 3:2), restored by a recorded patch. See the sources section.

## 8. How to reproduce

```sh
git clone https://github.com/nicklecoder/bom-stylometry.git && cd bom-stylometry
uv sync --extra verbs            # Python 3.12; spaCy model for per-verb and greek-egeneto
uv run bomstylo fetch            # download, check by sha256, prepare
uv run bomstylo verify           # prepared files match their pins
uv run bomstylo run              # every analysis, in dependency order (about 6 minutes)
uv run bomstylo status           # all should read "current"
uv run bomstylo report wayhi     # rebuilds this file
```

Each result file records the hashes of everything it was computed from. If a rerun changes a
headline number outside its previous interval, `uv run bomstylo record` says so in the Requiem
record. The analyses are listed, with their inputs, in [`ANALYSES.md`](../ANALYSES.md).
